name: The Severance Bloc
motto: What we built, we take with us.
description:
The Severance Bloc emerged from the catastrophic 2181 restructuring of TESSERA CORPONATION's Laceworks division, when TESSERA quietly dissolved its entire Applied Infrastructure wing — roughly 1,400 engineers, systems architects, and embedded contractors — via automated termination protocols rather than face negotiated buyouts. The affected workers, many of whom held proprietary neural imprints of TESSERA's internal logistics architecture, found themselves simultaneously unemployed, locked out of their augmentation licenses, and legally barred from practicing their specializations under TESSERA's non-compete clauses. Seventeen of them, led by a logistics architect named Priya Sundaram, refused to comply. They reverse-engineered their own augmentation locks, pooled their severance litigation funds, and began operating as an independent infrastructure consultancy out of a decommissioned TESSERA subnode in the deep Laceworks. The corponation pursued them through civil litigation for three years before quietly dropping the case — by which point the Bloc had become too embedded in the district's actual functioning to remove without causing a cascade failure.

Today the Severance Bloc operates as a mid-tier power in the Laceworks and spills into the industrial margins of Old Harbor, providing infrastructure services — power routing, water reclamation, data conduit maintenance — that the corponations officially control but practically neglect. They are not a criminal organization in the traditional sense; they are a competing service provider that operates without corporate sanction, which in GLMZ amounts to the same thing. Their client base includes tiered-two and tiered-three citizens, small-scale operators, and anyone who finds TESSERA's legitimate pricing structure prohibitive. They have developed a reputation for reliability that their corporate competitors quietly envy and publicly denounce.

What distinguishes the Bloc from other infrastructure-adjacent factions is their obsessive institutional culture around documentation and precedent. Every action they take is logged, archived, and stored in distributed redundancy across member-held wetware. They do not operate on handshakes. They operate on contracts — meticulously drafted, legally arguable documents that they have, on three separate occasions, successfully used in GLMZ's corporate arbitration courts. They are not revolutionaries. They are disgruntled professionals who have decided that professionalism is a weapon.
ideology: The Severance Bloc does not espouse liberation or systemic overthrow. Their ideology is closer to aggressive labor formalism: the belief that skilled workers who hold institutional knowledge are, in a practical sense, the institution, and that the legal architecture of corporate sovereignty is a set of rules that can be learned, exploited, and turned against its authors. They believe in the sanctity of the contract above all else — not as a corporate instrument, but as the only enforceable form of mutual obligation that exists in a city without public law. Many members have developed a secondary ideological strand that treats infrastructure itself as a commons — not owned by those who built it, but by those who maintain and depend on it — which brings them into uncomfortable proximity with more radical positions they officially reject.
territory: Primarily the Laceworks, specifically the mid-tier conduit networks and reclamation substations that TESSERA's official maintenance crews have chronically underfunded. Secondary presence in the industrial waterfront of Old Harbor, where they manage power and water routing for several independent manufacturing concerns. They maintain a hardened archive node in Substation Null that they lease from a third party and treat as sovereign ground.
leadership:
Flat council of nine elected department leads, called the Board — deliberately ironic nomenclature. Decisions require a recorded majority vote. The founding member Priya Sundaram holds a permanent advisory seat with no voting authority, a distinction she insisted on herself.

methods: Offering infrastructure services — power, water, data routing — at below-market rates to clients priced out of the corporate service tier
Maintaining meticulous contractual documentation on all operations to create legal defensibility in corporate arbitration
Leveraging members' proprietary neural imprints of TESSERA internal systems for competitive diagnostic and repair advantages
Embedding Bloc-maintained hardware alongside or within TESSERA infrastructure to create dependency relationships that make removal costly
Filing targeted arbitration claims against TESSERA for service negligence when Bloc infrastructure compensates for documented corporate failures
Recruiting specifically from the pool of terminated or license-locked TESSERA and PALLADIAN CONSTRUCTION workers
Running encrypted contract escrow services as a secondary revenue stream for unaffiliated operators in the Laceworks
resources: Extensive institutional knowledge of TESSERA's Laceworks infrastructure encoded in member wetware
A network of maintained power and water conduit infrastructure across the mid-Laceworks
The Substation Null archive node, housing their full legal and operational documentation
A small but capable legal fund built from successful arbitration awards
Relationships with independent manufacturing operators in Old Harbor who provide materials and fabrication support
Proprietary diagnostic augmentation tools developed in-house from reverse-engineered TESSERA equipment
A growing roster of 340 active members with specialized infrastructure expertise

relationships.description: TESSERA regards the Severance Bloc as an ongoing intellectual property violation and an intolerable affront to corporate authority. The Bloc regards TESSERA as a former employer that committed breach of contract first. Both are correct. TESSERA periodically attempts to dislodge Bloc infrastructure through technical means or contracted pressure; the Bloc responds with arbitration filings and infrastructure withdrawal threats timed to cause maximum disruption.

PALLADIAN has hired the Bloc quietly on three occasions for infrastructure assessment work in contested Laceworks zones where TESSERA's jurisdiction is ambiguous. Neither party acknowledges these arrangements publicly. PALLADIAN appreciates the Bloc's competence and resents TESSERA's monopolistic tendencies but will not formally align with an unsanctioned operator.

The Bloc's power routing operations in the Laceworks occasionally tap OUROBOROS distribution lines in ways that OUROBOROS considers unauthorized load-sharing and the Bloc considers compensated service agreements with downstream clients. There is ongoing low-level friction and occasional equipment sabotage that neither side has formally attributed.

The Cartographers have purchased infrastructure survey data from the Bloc on multiple occasions and have provided navigational intelligence for Bloc operations in Old Harbor's flooded sub-levels. The relationship is purely commercial and both parties prefer it that way.

The Collective views the Severance Bloc as a potential ideological ally who consistently refuses the invitation. The Bloc views the Collective as people who will get them killed. There is occasional cooperation on specific labor actions but the Bloc refuses to be publicly associated with anything the Collective does that could compromise their arbitration standing.

story_hooks: A Bloc member's neural archive contains a fragment of TESSERA infrastructure data that inadvertently documents a TESSERA cover-up of a fatal Laceworks maintenance failure — TESSERA wants it deleted, the Bloc wants to weaponize it in arbitration, and someone else entirely wants to sell it to VANTABLACK MEDIA

The Bloc's Substation Null archive node goes dark without warning; investigation reveals it was not attacked but voluntarily sealed by a Bloc insider who has defected — and taken a copy of the full member roster

PALLADIAN CONSTRUCTION approaches the players to broker a formal service agreement between the Bloc and PALLADIAN for a major Laceworks expansion project, which would legitimize the Bloc but require them to formally sever ties with several of their current clients

A wave of TESSERA-locked augmentation refugees from a newly terminated division arrives in the Laceworks seeking Bloc membership; the Bloc suspects at least some are TESSERA plants but cannot afford to turn away the expertise

Yael Morin has discovered a precedent in GLMZ's corporate charter that could theoretically allow the Bloc to petition for provisional corponation status — a move that would either legitimize them permanently or make them a target for every faction with an interest in keeping the power structure intact

The Bloc's below-market service rates have destabilized a Laceworks neighborhood economy in ways nobody anticipated, and a tiered-three citizens' council is demanding the Bloc accept accountability structures that would fundamentally compromise their operational independence
